item.title: Our failure to contain dengue
item.description:
The grim toll of Bangladesh’s ongoing dengue crisis continues to rise, exposing a chronic failure of public health management and municipal governance.
With the national death toll climbing past 280 as of October 6, daily hospitalizations nearing 2,000, and a sharp spike in infections hitting regional hubs like Chittagong, what should be a manageable seasonal illness has once again transformed into a deadly public health emergency.
That September registered as the deadliest month of the year proves that official interventions remain woefully inadequate, reactive, and out of step with reality.
The current surge also highlights a persistent breakdown in vector control and local administration oversight. Across Dhaka, Chittagong, and rural districts, residents routinely report invisible city corporation workers, irregular fogging drives, and unmonitored stagnant water at construction sites and public spaces.
While municipal authorities predictably shift blame onto public carelessness, the reality from finger pointing is more suffering and death - an outcome nobody wants in the country.
As such, we need an administrative apparatus that does not act only after hospital wards overflow. Spraying ineffective larvicides or launching sporadic "crash programs" after the peak transmission season takes hold is an exercise in public relations, not public health.
Simultaneously, we do need more public awareness and recognition that mosquitoes must be stopped from breeding.
Ultimately, as has been stated numerous times, dengue has long moved on from being an unexpected annual surprise. It is, and has been for some time now, an endemic threat that requires year-round, science-driven mitigation.
We need our health authorities across the country to abandon their seasonal complacency. Treating human lives as acceptable collateral in what has become an annual administrative failure is unacceptable. We must act with the urgency needed to halt this preventable devastation.

item.title: Lethal force is not the answer
item.description:
The latest incident of firing by the Indian Border Security Force (BSF), which left two Indian nationals critically injured, serves as another grim reminder of a persistent, unacceptable crisis along the Bangladesh-India frontier.
This recent shooting underscores a broader, fundamental reality: The routine resort to lethal force by Indian border guards is a systemic issue that threatens human lives and undermines regional stability, regardless of the victims' nationality.
That reports also suggest that the BSF personnel detained them and tried to push them into Bangladesh, and fired after they resisted, is also deeply concerning, and needs clarification and investigation into the matter.
For years, high-level diplomatic meetings and ministerial summits between Dhaka and New Delhi have concluded with repeated assurances that non-lethal weapons would be prioritized and border fatalities brought down to zero.
Yet, on the ground, it is safe to say that trigger-happy responses remain far too frequent for comfort.
Tragic incidents involving firearm usage along an international border, often over petty smuggling or unauthorized crossings, defy basic international law enforcement standards. Surely we can agree that lethal force must strictly be a measure of last resort against imminent threats to life.
This cycle of violence cannot be normalized and must be condemned by all. Border management between two neighbouring nations, that too with such deep economic and diplomatic ties, requires more restraint and operational discipline.
It is high time to move past platitudes and enforce strict accountability. BSF personnel who violate non-lethal mandates must face thorough, independent investigations and clear legal consequences.
Resorting to live ammunition against unarmed or fleeing individuals breeds public resentment, fuels cross-border tension, and ultimately undermines the spirit of bilateral cooperation. We expect better.

item.title: Three die of dengue in Khulna in 24 hours, 302 hospitalised
item.description:
The dengue outbreak continues to worsen in Khulna Division, with three more people dying of the mosquito-borne disease and 302 patients hospitalised in the last 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday.
Khulna Divisional Health Director Dr Sheikh Mosharraf Hossain disclosed the information on Tuesday afternoon.
According to the health department, two of the three deaths occurred at hospitals in Khulna district, while the other was reported at Khulna Medical College Hospital (KMCH). With the latest deaths, the dengue death toll in the division has reached 55 since January 1 this year.
Of the 302 newly hospitalised patients, 231 are receiving treatment at government hospitals and 71 at private facilities.
Khulna district recorded the highest number of new admissions at 143, followed by KMCH with 44, Bagerhat 35, Jessore 18, Narail 18, Satkhira 16, Magura 10, Meherpur eight, Kushtia seven and Chuadanga three.
Health department data show that 15,063 people have been infected with dengue in the division since the beginning of the year.
Of them, 13,379 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, while 1,263 patients are currently undergoing treatment at hospitals across the division.

item.title: LPG cylinders sell at Tk200-500 above govt-fixed price in Faridpur
item.description:
Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) cylinders are being sold at Tk200-500 above government-set prices in Faridpur, with consumers blaming inadequate market monitoring and alleged supply shortages.
The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) has raised the price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), setting the price of a 12kg cylinder at Tk 1,837, up from Tk 1,585.
Consumers in Faridpur town, upazila headquarters, and remote markets said they are often forced to pay more than the fixed price despite LPG cylinders being available.
Depending on brand and size, cylinders are currently selling for Tk2,000-2,500 in different markets across the district, locals said. Prices are reportedly even higher in some remote markets in Nagarkanda, Saltha and Madhukhali.
Consumers said the rising cost of LPG is adding to the financial pressure on households already struggling with higher prices of essential commodities.
Two autorickshaw drivers, a hotel owner and a homemaker on Mujib Road in Faridpur town said authorities should strengthen market monitoring and ensure LPG is sold at the fixed price.
The price hike is also affecting small businesses, particularly hotels, restaurants, food shops and tea stalls that rely on LPG for cooking.
Several traders in Nagarkanda market said LPG costs more in village markets than at the upazila headquarters, increasing their operating expenses and reducing profits.
“Cooking costs are rising with the price of gas. Other essentials have also become more expensive. Overall, it has become difficult to run the business as before,” a hotel owner said.
Retailers, however, attributed the higher prices to supply shortages. They said they sometimes have to buy cylinders at higher prices and incur additional transportation costs, making it difficult to sell them at government-set rates.
“We are also buying gas at higher prices. When supply is irregular, we sometimes have to incur additional costs to collect cylinders. We do not want to charge customers more deliberately,” a retailer said.
Locals also alleged that regular monitoring by the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection was lacking despite widespread complaints of overpricing. They called for regular drives to ensure LPG is sold at government-set prices.
Faridpur Additional District Magistrate Susmita Saha said instructions had been issued to all upazila nirbahi officers and executive magistrates to monitor LPG prices.

item.title: Fever in every house, symptoms that require caution
item.description:
Sabrina Akter brought her five-year-old daughter to the pediatric outpatient department of Chattogram Medical College Hospital. Her daughter’s fever had not subsided for several days, which eventually left Sabrina worried.

She became particularly concerned after hearing reports about dengue and measles infections in Chattogram and began to fear that her daughter’s fever might have a serious cause.

Sabrina Akter said she initially waited for two days. However, when the fever did not subside, she did not delay any further and took her daughter to hospital.

After consulting a physician, she felt somewhat reassured. The physician told her that her daughter did not have any serious complications and would recover with regular medication and proper care.

Sabrina Akter said she had also recently suffered from a fever. At the same time, she had been regularly hearing reports about dengue and measles infections in Chattogram.

News of people dying after getting fever, particularly in September, made her even more concerned. Therefore, when her daughter developed a fever, she considered consulting a physician the safest option rather than taking any risks.

However, Sabrina Akter is not alone. Patients of various ages visit the pediatric and medicine outpatient departments of Chattogram Medical College Hospital every day with symptoms such as fever, a runny nose, cough, sore throat and body aches.

Alongside children, young, middle-aged and elderly patients are also seeking medical advice for these symptoms. Some have had fever for several days, while others have experienced fever accompanied by a runny nose, cough or body aches.

Physicians say seasonal fever, colds, coughs and respiratory infections such as influenza are common during this period.

However, as dengue and measles infections are also circulating at the same time, people should not dismiss a fever as an ordinary seasonal illness.

If a child or person of any age develops persistent fever, a cold, cough or any other symptoms, they should seek medical advice when necessary.

Why fever is more common at this time of year

Physicians say the number of patients with fever, colds and coughs increases during this period of seasonal transition.

Changes in weather, fluctuations in temperature and infections caused by various viruses can lead to different respiratory infections at this time of year.

Children, in particular, are more prone to fever, colds and coughs. In many cases, these symptoms improve after a few days with proper care and treatment.

However, people should not assume that every fever is simply a common illness. Fever is not a disease itself; rather, it is a symptom of an underlying problem or infection in the body.

In addition to viral or bacterial infections, fever can result from inflammation, various illnesses or other physical problems. In some cases, an injury can also trigger fever as a result of an inflammatory response.

Physicians say there is no need to panic when a fever develops. At the same time, people should not completely ignore it by assuming that it is merely a seasonal problem.

When someone develops a fever, they should first get adequate rest. They should also take care to prevent dehydration. Regularly monitoring body temperature and watching for any new symptoms alongside the fever are also important.

To prevent dehydration, patients can have boiled water, oral rehydration solution, soup or other fluids. Parents should pay particular attention to ensuring that children receive adequate food and fluids.

People should not start taking different medicines on their own to reduce a fever. They should consult a physician if necessary.

Dengue infection raises alarm in Chattogram

Amid fever cases in households across Chattogram, concern over dengue is also growing. The experience of Md Abu Toyeb, who is receiving treatment in the Medicine Department of Chattogram General Hospital, reflects the situation. He was admitted to the hospital with a fever after travelling from Banshkhali upazila.

Abu Toyeb said he initially developed pain throughout his body, followed by a gradual onset of fever. As the fever and body aches worsened, he eventually decided to seek hospital treatment. Tests later confirmed that he had dengue.

Conversations with several other patients receiving treatment at the hospital revealed that they, too, had various dengue symptoms alongside fever.

Some came to the hospital for tests after hearing reports of fever spreading from household to household and increasing dengue infections.

Tests later confirmed dengue in some of them. After receiving treatment, their physical condition has improved somewhat compared with before.

According to data from the Chattogram Civil Surgeon’s Office, 4,466 people in the district had contracted dengue by 30 September this year. Of them, 2,430 were infected in September alone.

Sixteen people died of dengue during the same month. By 30 September, the total number of dengue deaths in the district this year had reached 21. This means September accounted for a large proportion of the year’s total infections and deaths.

Dengue infections are also increasing in the city. Hospitals across Chattogram saw a rise in the number of dengue patients in September.

According to figures from 30 September, Chattogram Medical College Hospital admitted 31 new dengue patients that day, taking the total number of patients receiving treatment there to 87. By 30 September this year, 1,851 dengue patients had been admitted to the hospital, while 1,669 had recovered.

Amid the rising infections, Chattogram City Corporation has also been conducting drives to identify breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes across the city.

The corporation said mosquito-control measures alone are not enough to control dengue; preventing stagnant water from accumulating in and around homes is also crucial. Authorities have intensified special mosquito-control drives and cleanliness campaigns in high-risk areas of the city.

Growing concern over measles

Alongside dengue, parents are becoming increasingly concerned about measles as children develop rashes with fever. Children with fever, colds, coughs and rashes are turning up at various government and private hospitals for treatment. While tests have confirmed measles in some cases, many children are being kept under observation on suspicion of having the disease.

According to data from the Chattogram Civil Surgeon’s Office, 255 people suspected of having measles were admitted to hospitals across Chattogram district on 30 September.

Of them, 250 were in hospitals in the city. By that day, the number of patients admitted to hospitals with suspected measles had reached 9,006. However, tests have confirmed measles in 743 patients so far.

During the same period, 26 deaths were reported among people suspected of having measles.

A recent study conducted in Chattogram has further highlighted the reasons for concern over measles among children. The third research project of Asperia Health Research and Development Foundation collected samples from various hospitals in Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar and Cumilla.

The researchers collected 300 samples in total. Of these, 196 were samples from children only, while 104 were samples from mothers and children.

One of the concerning findings of the study was that 59.4 per cent of children with measles were found to have contracted the infection while staying at a healthcare centre or hospital. The researchers said a shortage of beds and multiple children staying in the same space at hospitals could increase the risk of infection.

Among the infected children, 46 per cent were under nine months old. In other words, they contracted measles before reaching the scheduled age for the first measles vaccine under the routine immunisation programme.

For this reason, the research team recommended lowering the age for measles vaccination to six months. The study also found that 51 of the 196 children, or 31 per cent, had moderate to severe malnutrition.

Lead researcher Kamrun Nahar said, “In the case of measles, not only the infection but also a child’s nutritional status is associated with the severity and complications of the disease. The study found moderate to severe malnutrition in a large proportion of the affected children. Therefore, alongside vaccination to prevent measles, greater emphasis should be placed on ensuring adequate nutrition for children and providing regular vitamin A capsules.”

Neither panic nor neglect

According to physicians, the cause of fever can vary from person to person. In some cases, it may be part of a common seasonal infection, while in others it may indicate dengue, measles or another illness.

Therefore, it is important to pay attention not only to the severity of the fever but also to other accompanying symptoms and how long the fever has persisted.

Physicians say people should first monitor their physical condition rather than panic when they develop a fever.

However, if symptoms such as breathing difficulties, extreme weakness, repeated vomiting, seizures, unusual drowsiness, bleeding, reduced urine output or a rash develop alongside the fever, they should seek medical advice without delay.

Children showing these symptoms require even more prompt medical attention.

Kazi Ashik Aman, resident medical officer (RMO) at Chattogram General Hospital, said, “There is no need to panic simply because you have a fever. During the first two to three days of fever, you should monitor other symptoms. You should consume adequate fluids during this period. If necessary, you should undergo tests and receive treatment after consulting a physician. Do not take any medicine on your own.”

item.title: Emotion, tears as Messi retires from Argentina national team
item.description:
TOPSHOT-FBL-FRIENDLY-ARG-BEN

Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as ‘The Last Tango’.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina team-mates made its way through crowds of wellwishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word “Gracias” (Thank You) above the football superstar’s No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read -- “The Malvinas are Argentine” -- the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute -- in tribute to Messi’s famous shirt number -- for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

‘Gave it my all’

At the final whistle a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi’s image and thanking the eight-time Ballon D’Or-winner for his career.

Messi’s farewell came two and a half months after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote at the time.

Before Tuesday’s game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

“To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!,” he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed “The joy of my life.”

Former Barcelona team-mate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

“It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi’s departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country’s 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona’s heir.

“I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn’t bother me at all that he’s leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest,” Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

item.title: LPG prices high in Bangladesh
item.description:
The set price for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) used for cooking is higher in Bangladesh compared to neighbouring countries.

In Bangladesh, the set price per kg of LPG is approximately Tk 153 Taka. In Kolkata, India, it’s Tk 87. The fixed price of LPG is also lower in countries like Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal compared to Bangladesh.

In Bangladesh, the price is determined by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC). However, these prices are never implemented in the market.

For example, the fixed price for a 12-kg cylinder of gas is Tk 1,837, but in Dhaka, it is being sold at prices between Tk 2,300 and Tk 2,500.

Overall, it appears that people in Bangladesh have to buy cooking gas at a much higher price than in neighboring countries.

Both the government body BERC and the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection (DNCRP) have been unable to enforce even the high set prices. This issue is not new; it has been ongoing for many years.

There are approximately 10 million LPG users in the country. Among them, 80 per cent use it for household cooking purposes. The demand for LPG is now over 1.5 million tonnes per year. When LPG prices go up, the lower and middle class people struggle. Amidst high prices for electricity, fuel, and everyday commodities, the price of LPG is unrestrained.

Sazzadur Rahman, a private employee from Mirpur, Dhaka, told Prothom Alo that his family needs two cylinders (12 kg each) of LPG per month. Recently, he bought one cylinder for Tk 2,400.

He said that government agencies won't be able to enforce the fixed price, yet ordinary people will have to pay high taxes to double their salaries; that seems to be the fate.

Price comparison by country

Two types of gas are used for cooking in the country: pipeline natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas or LPG. Gas line installations in households have been halted since 2015. On the other hand, the demand for LPG is increasing.

Private companies primarily import LPG to meet the demand. Following a court order, BERC sets the price monthly. The agency has been setting the LPG prices since April 2021, aiming to provide cooking gas at affordable rates to the people.

Last Sunday, the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) announced the new LPG prices. The price for a 12-kg cylinder was set at Tk 1,837, an increase of Tk 252. Yesterday, a conversation about LPG prices took place at a retail seller’s shop in the Mohammadpur Housing Limited area. On the condition of anonymity, he said that the supply of LPG hasn’t increased. Even if they want 30 cylinders per day, they only receive 15. Each 12-kg cylinder is being sold at Tk 2,400.

According to data from the state-owned Indian oil company, IOC, each Indian state has different LPG prices. In Kolkata, the capital city of West Bengal, the retail price of a 14. 2-kg LPG cylinder is 968 Rupees. Therefore, the price per kg is 68.17 Rupees, which is Tk 87 in Bangladeshi currency. Prices are even lower in Delhi and Mumbai.

BERC Chairman Jalal Ahmed told Prothom Alo that comparing with India is challenging. In India, a government agency sells LPG, and they have more infrastructure capacity.

He said that primarily due to transport costs, the price is higher compared to other countries. There is land available at Maheshkhali’s Matarbari for the LPG company. If they set up a terminal, imports can be made with large ships. They have land in Chattogram by the Karnaphuli River, in Mongla of Bagerhat, and in Elenga of Tangail. They can create large warehouses that may take three to four years and then bring the price down like in other countries.

Meanwhile, the IOC website states that the current price has been effective since June and there is no subsidy included in these prices.

A Prothom Alo correspondent from Delhi reported that in India, there are two types of subsidies. One is that the government provides 300 Rupees per cylinder to the poor, sent as financial services through banks/mobile phones. On the other hand, the state-owned oil company IOC sometimes sells LPG cylinders to homes at a loss.

An article from the well-known Indian daily The Hindu says in September, the implicit subsidy amount on a 14. 2-kg cylinder was 210 Rupees. Calculations show that even without the subsidy, the price of a 12-kg cylinder hovers around Tk 1,300.

The website of the private company LAUGFS Gas in Sri Lanka mentions that there is some variation in LPG prices in different cities of the country. The price of a 12. 5-kg cylinder in the capital Colombo is 4,965 Rupees, equating to less than Tk 1,400 in Bangladeshi currency.

A report from the Pakistani newspaper The Dawn on 1 October stated that the Pakistan Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority increased LPG prices by 8 per cent. The price per kg was set at 279 Rupees.

After calculation, the price for a 12-kg cylinder comes to slightly less than Tk 1,500 in Bangladeshi currency.

Information from the Nepal Oil Corporation states that the price of a 14. 2-kg LPG cylinder in the country is 2,060 Rupees, which is slightly less than Tk 1,400 in Bangladeshi currency. Journalists in India, Sri Lanka, and Nepal have mentioned that LPG is roughly sold at the government-set price in these countries. In Pakistan, there are allegations of selling slightly above the set price. However, no country sells LPG at as high a price as Bangladesh.

Traders associated with LPG import and supply say that there are no terminals in the deep sea in the country. There is no capacity to store sufficient LPG. Therefore, it is imported in small ships, which incurs higher costs.

Former president of the LPG Operators Association of Bangladesh (LOAB) Azam J Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that due to infrastructural limitations and ship rental costs, Bangladesh is lagging behind in the competition. If a terminal were constructed in the deep sea and storage capacity increased, the price would also decrease in the country. He said that if the price goes up, demand goes down, so traders don’t want higher prices.

Supply hasn’t stabilised in the market

The reason for the LPG cylinder price rising to Tk 2,500 in two weeks is a decrease in supply. Conversations with LPG distributors and retailers in the market revealed that some companies started reducing supply from 20 September. Initially, the supply was reduced by 30 per cent. Later, it was gradually reduced by more than 50 per cent.

LOAB, the traders’ organisation, stated that in August, 158,000 metric tonnes of LPG was imported. The import quantity in September was 156,000 tonnes. This indicates that import levels are normal. Therefore, the organisation has warned everyone not to sell LPG at excessively high prices.

It was anticipated that the market price would stabilise following BERC’s price adjustments. According to business sources, after BERC increased the prices, the supply is now increasing. However, there is a long queue of waiting trucks, so it may take more than a week for supply to normalise.

In this regard, Azam J Chowdhury said that due to a shortage in pipeline gas supply, the demand for LPG in the industry has increased. As a result, although import is on track, residential supply has decreased. More imports are being increased. It will take a few days for supply to normalise.

Lower prices outside Dhaka

The BERC chairman and traders provided various reasons for the high LPG price in Bangladesh. After talking with them, inquiries at a shop in Battola area of Barishal city revealed that the price for 12-kg cylinders of Petromax, Sun, and Fresh brands is Tk 1,870, and Total Gas is Tk 1,920. The question is, why is the price Tk 400–500 more in Dhaka?

When Sazzadur Rahman, the private employee from Mirpur, Dhaka was informed about the situation, he told Prothom Alo that the market chaos is due to the failure of governmental agencies.

item.title: CUET VC withholds teachers’, officials’ salaries amid protests
item.description:
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) has remained closed for 15 days amid protests by teachers, students, officers and employees demanding the reinstatement of the recently outgoing vice-chancellor (VC).

The new VC has so far been unable to enter the campus because of the protests. However, despite being unable to go to the campus, he instructed the concerned bank by email to withhold the salaries and allowances of CUET teachers, officers and employees.

On 29 September, newly appointed VC Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam emailed Jayanta Bhowmik, manager of Sonali Bank’s CUET branch, instructing him to withhold the salaries of teachers, officers and employees.

The withholding of salaries and allowances has caused difficulties for CUET staff. Hindu teachers, officers and employees, in particular, are facing difficulties as the Durga Puja festival is approaching.

On 21 September, the authorities removed Professor Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem from the post of CUET vice-chancellor and appointed Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) as his replacement.

However, students launched a “complete shutdown” on 22 September, demanding Professor Abu Sadat’s reinstatement. Later, teachers, officers and employees also began a work abstention with the same demand.

Amid the protests by teachers, officers and employees, CUET’s new VC, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, joined the university on 24 September without going to the campus.

He said he had joined the university by sending his joining letter to the President and the Secretary of the Ministry of Education.

According to university sources, after receiving the email on 29 September, Jayanta Bhowmik, manager of Sonali Bank’s CUET branch, sent a reply to the new VC on 5 October.

He said he had received the salary bills for teachers, officers and employees bearing the signatures of the university’s Comptroller and Deputy Comptroller.

In response, the VC sent another email stating that sending salary bills to the bank without the VC’s prior approval was “unauthorised and illegal”.

In the email, the VC stated that under Section 13(7) of the CUET Act 2003, any financial transaction without the VC’s explicit approval was legally invalid.

He said that if any financial irregularity, undesirable situation or legal complication arose from such an unauthorised transaction, neither the VC nor the university authorities would bear any legal, administrative or financial liability.

Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, The new vice-chancellor of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET)I called the Comptroller and other relevant officials to a meeting, but none of them attended. I then emailed the bank manager.

He further stated that the two officials concerned would bear sole and full responsibility for any violation resulting from the preparation and submission of such unauthorised documents. He also said that Sonali Bank authorities would be held responsible for this.

When contacted, Jayanta Bhowmik, manager of Sonali Bank’s CUET branch, confirmed the authenticity of the email. He said, “The salaries have been withheld following the VC’s email. He sent emails informing Bangladesh Bank and everyone from Sonali Bank’s general manager to deputy general manager. The matter has been reported to the higher authorities, and a solution will come from there.”

The new vice-chancellor of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET), Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, told Prothom Alo, “I called the Comptroller and other relevant officials to a meeting, but none of them attended. I then emailed the bank manager. In the email, I stated that if any financial irregularity, undesirable situation or legal complication arose from the transaction, neither the vice-chancellor nor the university authorities would bear any legal, administrative or financial liability. The bank authorities suspended the salaries after seeing this email.”

Syed Mohammad Ikram, president of the CUET Officers’ Association, told Prothom Alo, “According to the prevailing rules, the vice-chancellor’s signature is not required to pay salaries and bonuses. If someone receives a salary increment or promotion, the vice-chancellor’s signature may be required. Salaries and allowances have been paid this way all along.”

However, Vice-Chancellor Sheikh Shariful Alam has claimed that the practice CUET has followed to disburse salaries until now is legally invalid.

He told Prothom Alo, “The way salaries were being paid until now was not legally valid. According to the rules, the vice-chancellor’s approval must be obtained. However, this rule has not been followed until now.”

Regarding the withholding of salaries and allowances, Samiun Basir, joint secretary of the CUET Teachers’ Association, told Prothom Alo, “According to CUET’s longstanding practice, the September salary bill was submitted through the Comptroller. However, because of the vice-chancellor’s intervention, no one has received their salary so far.”

He said, “The new vice-chancellor may have withheld the salaries to demonstrate his authority. If the way salaries were being paid until now was against the rules, then he should deduct all the salaries everyone has received so far. Everyone is on a work abstention, so why would they go to a meeting with him?”

item.title: Messi says Argentina retirement is “saddest day of my career”
item.description:
TOPSHOT-FBL-FRIENDLY-ARG-BEN

Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the "saddest day of my career" on Tuesday after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin.

Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and team-mates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina.

"It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years," Messi told the stadium.

"Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."

Messi said that returning to the Monumental -- where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup -- was bittersweet.

"Now I'm here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you.

"But now I'll be on that side (with the fans), supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united," he said.

Messi though said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina's campaign at this year's World Cup, where the South Americans battled through to the final only to lose to Spain.

Messi said the emotional roller coaster of that tournament -- which included a 2-1 defeat of bitter rivals England in the semi-final -- had taken a toll.

"Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through," said Messi.

"We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again.

"In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big.

"We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close."

item.title: Import duty on orange higher than on Mercedes cars
item.description:
So far, seven Tesla electric vehicles have been imported into Bangladesh. Depending on the year, importers had to pay duties and taxes equivalent to 89 to 92 per cent of the vehicles’ value.

In the current fiscal year, the rate will be 80 per cent for a US$50,000 Tesla. For a US$25,000 BYD or an electric vehicle in the same category, the rate will be 64 per cent.

Now, consider Mercedes-Benz cars. On 23 September, Rangs Motors Limited cleared three Mercedes-Benz cars manufactured in 2026 from Dhaka’s Kamalapur ICD.

Each car has a market value of around Tk 23.9 million. Importers had to pay duties and taxes equivalent to 96.10 per cent on these vehicles.

However, the import duty and tax burden on orange (locally known as Malta), a fruit commonly used as a dietary item for dengue patients, is even higher at 121.78 per cent.

Not only Tesla or Mercedes-Benz cars, but at least 146 categories of vehicles under different HS codes have lower import duties and taxes than orange, according to the tariff for the current fiscal year.

Touhidul Alam, organisational secretary of the Bangladesh Fresh Fruits Importers Association, told Prothom Alo, “No country in the world imposes such high duties and taxes on imported fruit. It is only in Bangladesh that fresh fruits, including orange, face higher duties and taxes than luxury cars.”

Khondaker Golam Moazzem, president of research organisation Knowledge Hub Institute TrustThe high duties and taxes on orange, which is used as a dietary item for patients, while some categories of cars considered luxury goods face lower duties and taxes, show that the current tariff structure lacks balance.

Recently, reduced imports pushed the retail price of orange up to Tk 480–520 per kilogram. However, its import-stage price was Tk 87 per kilogram, on which the duty and tax amounted to around Tk 107.

This brought orange’s high duty and tax rate back into discussion. However, after supplies increased, the price of orange fell to Tk 400 per kilogram.

In the 2006–07 fiscal year, the total tax burden on imported orange stood at 59.25 per cent. The burden then increased gradually, reaching 89.32 per cent by the 2021–22 fiscal year.

At the time, duties and taxes amounted to around Tk 38 per kilogram. Amid the dollar crisis, the then government imposed regulatory duties on fruit imports in May 2022 to discourage imports. As a result, the total duty and tax burden on orange rose to around 114 per cent.

During the interim government in the middle of the 2024–25 fiscal year, the authorities raised the tax burden further to 136 per cent. Fruit importers staged protests against the move.

The authorities later reduced some of the additional duties and taxes in March 2025. From the 2025–26 fiscal year, the total duty and tax burden on orange was set at 121.78 per cent, and the rate remains in effect.

23 times higher than in the US

The United States is one of the leading producers of orange. Although the country produces and exports orange, it also imports the fruit. The standard duty rate on orange in the United States is 1.9 cents per kilogram.

In addition, imports of orange from 16 countries and territories enjoy duty-free access. According to the United States International Trade Commission, the average effective tariff rate on orange stood at 5.19 per cent in the first six months of this year. By comparison, the duty and tax burden in Bangladesh is around 23 times higher.

According to information on the Indian Revenue Department’s website, neighbouring India also imposes a basic duty of 30 per cent on imported orange. Including other taxes, the total tax burden is around 33 per cent.

Junaidul Haque, a fruit importer and publicity secretary of the Chattogram Fruit Traders Association, told Prothom Alo that importers previously had to pay around Tk 750,000 in duties and taxes for each container of orange.

They now have to pay Tk 2.8 million to Tk 2.9 million. He said the high duties and taxes on fruit ultimately affect consumers as well as businesses.

Recommendation to rationalise duty and tax rates

After the authorities increased duties and taxes on fresh fruit, the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission recommended reducing them in a letter sent to the National Board of Revenue (NBR) on 17 February 2025.

The letter stated that fresh fruit is an essential food item. It also noted that the National Tariff Policy provides for the imposition of regulatory duties only when necessary.

In the 2006–07 fiscal year, the total tax burden on imported orange stood at 59.25 per cent. The burden then increased gradually, reaching 89.32 per cent by the 2021–22 fiscal year. At the time, duties and taxes amounted to around Tk 38 per kilogram.

Based on these two arguments, the commission recommended reducing duties and taxes on fresh fruit.

Khondaker Golam Moazzem, president of research organisation Knowledge Hub Institute Trust, told Prothom Alo that the authorities had increased duties and taxes on fruit, including orange, to discourage imports and prevent the country’s foreign exchange reserves from declining further.

He said the measure was not intended to protect the domestic market or increase revenue.

Although the reserve situation is not yet comfortable, it has improved compared with the past. Therefore, considering public health concerns, the duty and tax rates on orange should be rationalised.

Khondaker Golam Moazzem further said, “The high duties and taxes on orange, which is used as a dietary item for patients, while some categories of cars considered luxury goods face lower duties and taxes, show that the current tariff structure lacks balance.”

item.title: When the customers become students
item.description:
The moment the door opened and I stepped inside, the aroma of freshly baked buns greeted me. Laughter, conversation and a flurry of activity filled the room. Some were kneading flour, while others were learning the techniques of making buns.

In one corner, buns were baking in the oven. There was little doubt that I had arrived at the right place. On 3 October, Tingama Restaurant in Banani hosted a one-day ‘Cheery Workshop’.

Ten people took part in the workshop organised by baker Tanzima Islam. Although they varied in age, they shared one thing in common: they were all longtime customers of Tanzima’s.

They had been missing the food she used to make ever since she moved to Australia nearly a year ago. They would regularly order patties, chicken buns, brownies and other treats from Tanzima’s ‘Cheery Chef’ page for various family occasions. After she moved abroad, they were deprived of those familiar flavours.

So when they learned that Tanzima would be returning to Bangladesh for 12 days, it was the customers themselves who asked her to organise a workshop for them. The event was arranged in response to that request. Throughout the day, the participants learnt how to prepare some of Tanzima’s signature items, including patties, chicken buns and brownies.

Tanzima grew up surrounded by cooking from an early age. Her mother used to prepare all sorts of food at home. Even biscuits were never bought from outside; they were made at home. Her father, too, is a good cook.

Although the kitchen was familiar territory, Tanzima did not take up baking herself until much later, during the Covid-19 pandemic. Amid the difficult circumstances of the pandemic, she wanted to find something she could do with her family to lift their spirits. That was how her baking journey began.

What started as a hobby gradually became something more. Encouraged by the appreciation she received from her family, Tanzima decided to take it further. After the pandemic ended, she launched her ‘Cheery Chef’ page. It did not take long for her to win a warm response from customers.

Tanzima now works with bakery and pastry products as a supervisor at a bakery called ‘32 Bakehouse’ in Sydney. She also hopes to do something new in Bangladesh when she returns, while maintaining the bond she has built with her old customers.

“I don’t want the relationship I have built with my customers to be lost because of the distance,” Tanzima says. “That is the main reason behind organising this workshop. I am also very happy to have the opportunity to spend time with them again and teach them, hands-on, how I make these foods.

“I am grateful to Tingama Restaurant as well for giving me the opportunity to organise the workshop in such a beautiful and warm environment.”

item.title: Emotion, tears as Messi retires from Argentina national team
item.description:
Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.
In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.
Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.
But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as 'The Last Tango'.
Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina team-mates made its way through crowds of wellwishers en route to the stadium.
Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.
Shortly before kick off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word "Gracias" (Thank You) above the football superstar's No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.
Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read - "The Malvinas are Argentine" - the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.
The match was halted in the 10th minute -- in tribute to Messi's famous shirt number -- for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.
He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.
At the final whistle a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi's image and thanking the eight-time Ballon D'Or-winner for his career.
Messi's farewell came two and a half months after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.
"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote at the time.
Before Tuesday's game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.
Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.
"To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!," he joked.
Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed "The joy of my life."
Former Barcelona team-mate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.
"It's not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more," he said.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
Messi's departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country's 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona's heir.
"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.
During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

item.title: ‘I leave grateful, proud and at peace’: Messi’s full farewell speech
item.description:
Lionel Messi has officially said goodbye to the Argentina national team after two decades in the Albiceleste shirt. On Tuesday night, Argentina beat Benin 3-0 at the Monumental in Messi’s farewell match, with the captain scoring once and providing two assists.
The night had already turned into a celebration before kickoff, with singers performing for the packed stadium and tributes continuing after the final whistle. But once the festivities were over, Messi took the microphone to say goodbye to the supporters who had come to share his final night in an Argentina shirt.
Speaking in Spanish, Messi reflected on his extraordinary journey with the national team, the teammates who fought alongside him, the supporters who followed Argentina around the world and the dream of becoming world champions. He also revealed that his father was the first person who came to his mind during the emotional moment.
Here is Messi’s full farewell speech, translated into English:
"I have nothing left to do but thank this shirt. For 20 years, even through the worst moments, I never stopped fighting, pushing forward, giving everything I had and wanting to be here.
"Not coming here anymore and no longer being with the Argentina National Team is going to hurt a lot. If it were up to me, I would love to be here for my entire life, because playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing there is.
"I think I’m talking more than ever today because I simply don’t want this moment to end.
"But I think the time has come for me to retire. The last World Cup took a lot out of us after everything we went through. We arrived in the final with just enough left in us, but we fought until the very end, like we always did.
"We came very close to winning it again, and despite everything that was said about us, nothing strange happened. The match against England took a lot out of us because we gave absolutely everything.
"In 2022, we had the dream of fulfilling not only my dream, but the dream of an entire country: becoming world champions again. And we did it.
"We won the World Cup, the Copa América, the Finalissima… I’m incredibly grateful for everything I experienced with this National Team.
"But this journey wasn’t only about 2022 or this last World Cup. So many teammates fought alongside me for this shirt long before we finally became world champions. Never doubt how much every one of them fought and gave for Argentina.
"It was a privilege and an honor to share the pitch with all of my teammates and to share so much of our lives together away from football. Every time we stepped onto the pitch, I knew we could compete against anyone because I had warriors beside me who were willing to leave absolutely everything out there.
"To achieve the biggest things, you need a strong group. And it’s during the most difficult moments that you truly discover what kind of team you have. That’s one of the biggest reasons we were able to achieve everything we did.
"And especially to this group: THANK YOU. They helped me fulfill the dream I had since I was a child. They helped me become a world champion.
"I also want to thank the people. I was lucky enough to play in so many cities across Argentina, and everywhere I went, I received an incredible amount of love.
"Throughout all these years, wherever we played in the world, the stadiums were always full of Argentinians. No matter the match or the distance, people made an enormous effort to be there. We know how difficult that is. Wherever we went in the world, it felt like we were playing at home because we could always feel your support.
"And that support has to continue. Difficult moments will come, and those are the moments when you have to support the team more than ever. You need strong, united groups because there will always be people who want to see the National Team fail, and we can’t give them that satisfaction.
"Here, in this stadium, I experienced one of the happiest days of my life: our first match at home after becoming world champions. It was beautiful. And today might be one of the saddest because I’m standing here saying goodbye.
"I’m going to miss all of you so much, but I’ll always be on your side. I’ll be supporting these boys and everyone who comes after them.
"There are so many emotions going through me right now. I’m surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad.
"I’m going to miss playing here so much. I love you all, and I’m proud to be Argentine.
"I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything."
After 20 years, Messi’s journey with the Argentina national team is over.
He leaves behind a legacy crowned by the 2021 Copa América, the 2022 Finalissima and, most importantly, the 2022 World Cup — the trophy he had dreamed of winning for himself and his country.
His final words at the Monumental, however, were not about the trophies. They were a thank-you to the shirt, his teammates and the millions of Argentinians who stood by him through every high and low.
And with a final “Thank you for everything,” Messi said goodbye to the national team he had represented since 2005.

item.title: Dhaka air pollution worsens, ranks 3rd globally
item.description:
Dhaka ranked third among the world's most polluted cities on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 173 at 10:10am.
The air quality was classified as ‘unhealthy’, meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked first with an AQI score of 210, while Singapore in Singapore ranked second with a score of 176.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', while levels above 301 are deemed 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: The woman who refused to disappear
item.description:
“Till now, I have created stories based on lives of other people, but this time I have been so bold as to write my own.”
There is a reason Mannu Bhandari calls it an act of boldness. For a South Asian woman, writing her own story has never been a simple literary exercise.
Women are raised to carry families, preserve reputations and absorb pain without leaving a record of it. Silence is often mistaken for grace; endurance is celebrated more readily than honesty.
Even women who write are expected to disguise themselves behind fiction, to soften uncomfortable truths until they become palatable.
To write openly about marriage, loneliness and disappointment is to risk being judged before being understood. A woman’s life has long been narrated by others—by families, by society, by history.
To take back that narrative is not merely an artistic choice. It is an act of reclamation.
It is from that place of reclamation that ‘This Too Is a Story,’ translated by Poonam Saxena, unfolds.
One of Hindi literature’s most celebrated voices turns inward, not to preserve a public legacy or settle old scores, but to understand what remained of herself after years of emotional compromise.
The result is an autobiography of extraordinary clarity that speaks not only to the making of a writer but to the quiet unmaking of a woman inside the institution that promised to complete her.
The memoir’s first revelation arrives before Bhandari’s own voice does.
Saxena’s translator’s note quietly alters the way Bhandari’s fiction is read.
Readers who have long admired the emotional precision of her stories may find themselves returning to them with different eyes.
The women who populate her fiction—their loneliness, their restraint, the invisible negotiations that shape their lives—begin to resemble emotional self-portraits.
It is not that her stories become autobiography. Rather, the memoir reveals how deeply life had always nourished her fiction. The distance between author and character suddenly feels much smaller.
That realization lends the memoir an added poignancy.
For generations of women across South Asia, marriage has been presented as fulfilment. It is wrapped in rituals, blessings and promises of permanence. Girls grow up hearing that every achievement ultimately leads to this destination.
What receives far less attention is the quiet arithmetic that follows: the ambitions postponed, the identities absorbed into another household, the creative selves asked to wait until everyone else’s needs have been met.
Bhandari writes from within that reality.
The memoir does not rely on dramatic confrontations or spectacular suffering. Its emotional force comes from the slow erosion of selfhood.
Creative work gives way to domestic negotiations. Emotional exhaustion becomes routine. Compromise ceases to feel like sacrifice because it has become ordinary.
Patriarchy rarely announces itself in Bhandari’s life with theatrical cruelty. It appears instead through repetition, expectation and the countless invisible concessions that slowly reshape a woman’s sense of herself.
The book’s most devastating pages arrive near its end.
Bhandari writes of longing to write again. Every day begins with a promise to return to her desk. Every evening ends with that promise deferred.
The repetition is almost unbearable because writing has ceased to be a profession; it has become the measure of a life that once felt fully inhabited.
Watching one of Hindi literature’s finest voices struggle to reclaim the very impulse that defined her is to witness a loss that extends beyond literature. It is the erosion of identity itself.
There are many ways a woman can be silenced. Some are loud. Others happen so gradually that they become indistinguishable from daily life.
Measured purely by volume, Mannu Bhandari’s literary career was not among the longest of her generation.
Its influence, however, far exceeded its size. Like Ismat Chughtai and Amrita Pritam, Bhandari transformed the ordinary into the unforgettable.
Her prose never demanded attention through ornament. Its power rested in emotional accuracy, in the ability to expose entire worlds through conversations at dining tables and silences inside bedrooms.
Even Rajnigandha , adapted into Basu Chatterjee’s beloved film, endures because it trusted the emotional complexity of ordinary lives over grand drama.
This memoir reveals the cost of writing with such honesty.
Its most heartbreaking chapter is not about the collapse of a marriage but about the loneliness that followed. Friendships frayed as people gravitated towards literary influence and professional power, leaving Bhandari increasingly isolated. The loss extended beyond home into the very community that should have recognised her worth. It is a familiar pattern.
Women are often expected to survive heartbreak with dignity while institutions quietly continue to reward the men at their centre.
What gives ‘This Too Is a Story’ its remarkable dignity is its refusal to seek revenge. Bhandari does not simplify the past into heroes and villains.
She writes with restraint, examining herself as closely as everyone around her. That honesty gives the memoir its moral authority.
Poonam Saxena’s translation deserves equal praise. It preserves the remarkable plainness of Bhandari’s prose without sacrificing its emotional depth.
Every sentence carries the quiet confidence of a writer who has no interest in embellishment because the truth requires none.
The book closes, but its questions remain.
How many stories have disappeared inside marriages celebrated as happy endings?
How many writers, artists and thinkers have quietly abandoned parts of themselves because sacrifice was mistaken for love?
How many women have been told that marriage would make them whole, only to discover that it demanded they become smaller?
‘This Too Is a Story’ is more than the autobiography of Mannu Bhandari.
It is an elegy for the unwritten books, the interrupted mornings and the creative lives that never reached their fullest expression. It leaves behind grief, certainly, but grief soon hardens into anger—not only for one extraordinary writer, but for every woman whose story has been edited by expectation long before she had the chance to write it herself.
Namrata is Founder of Keemiya Creative & Bookbots India.

item.title: Messi says Argentina retirement is 'saddest day of my career'
item.description:
Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the "saddest day of my career" on Tuesday after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin.
Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and team-mates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina.
"It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years," Messi told the stadium.
"Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here.
"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."
Messi said that returning to the Monumental -- where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup -- was bittersweet.
"Now I'm here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you.
"But now I'll be on that side (with the fans), supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united," he said.
Messi though said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina's campaign at this year's World Cup, where the South Americans battled through to the final only to lose to Spain.
Messi said the emotional roller coaster of that tournament -- which included a 2-1 defeat of bitter rivals England in the semi-final -- had taken a toll.
"Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through," said Messi.
"We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again.
"In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big.
"We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close."

item.title: Private universities are challenging old academic hierarchies
item.description:
The latest Times Higher Education rankings offer Bangladesh’s private universities something more valuable than a place on an international table: They offer evidence that the country’s higher education landscape is changing.
The change is not simply about private universities moving upward while public universities move downward. It is about a new competition emerging in Bangladeshi higher education, where institutional ambition, research capacity, international engagement, and responsiveness to changing academic expectations increasingly determine visibility.
For years, the conventional hierarchy of Bangladeshi universities seemed almost unquestionable. Public universities, particularly the older ones, occupied the symbolic high ground. Their historical importance, academic traditions, alumni networks and contributions to national life gave them an authority that newer institutions could not easily challenge.
Private universities were often regarded as commercially driven alternatives, useful for students who could not enter the public system or preferred a different academic environment. That perception is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.
The Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027 provide an important indication of why. Of the four Bangladeshi universities placed in the 801 to 1000 band, three are private: American International University-Bangladesh, Daffodil International University, and North South University. Jahangirnagar University is the only public university in that group.
This does not mean that private universities have suddenly become superior to public universities in every respect. Rankings cannot settle such a complicated question. But they do tell us something important: Several private institutions have developed measurable strengths that allow them to compete with universities carrying decades of institutional history.
That development deserves neither exaggerated celebration nor instinctive suspicion. It deserves serious examination.
One reason private universities have been able to advance is that many of them were born into a different academic environment. They did not inherit the enormous weight of tradition that older public universities carry. They had to build their reputations almost from scratch.
That created pressure to establish recognisable academic brands, attract qualified faculty, develop modern infrastructure, maintain relationships with industry and present themselves as internationally-oriented institutions. In an increasingly competitive higher education market, standing still has consequences.
The same shift is visible beyond conventional university rankings. IUBAT, for instance, has built a notable record in sustainability and environmental performance, ranking 1st in Bangladesh, 113th in Asia, and 197th globally in the 2026 UI GreenMetric World University Rankings among 2016 universities from 110 countries.
Such achievements are particularly noteworthy because sustainability remains an area where many of Bangladesh's public universities have yet to establish comparable international visibility. The point is not that private universities have solved the problem, but that some are showing how institutional commitment can turn sustainability from a ceremonial slogan into measurable practice.
There is also a generational difference in institutional thinking. Many private universities were established when globalization, digital technology, and international academic mobility were already becoming central to higher education.
Their institutional cultures therefore developed around a world in which universities were expected to communicate internationally, collaborate across borders, engage with employers, and demonstrate measurable academic performance.
For institutions seeking students in a competitive market, international recognition is not merely a matter of prestige. It is part of the product they are offering.
This is where the ranking story becomes more interesting. Times Higher Education does not assess universities simply by asking how famous they are. Its indicators consider teaching, research environment, research quality, industry engagement and international outlook.
A university therefore cannot rely indefinitely on its historical reputation. Reputation may open a door, but research output, academic infrastructure and international engagement increasingly determine whether the door remains open.
The performance of private universities should consequently be understood as a challenge to complacency across the entire sector. If a relatively young institution can enter the same ranking band as universities with much longer histories, the question is not only what the younger institution is doing right. The more uncomfortable question is what established institutions may be doing too slowly.
This does not make the rankings an unquestionable measure of educational quality. University rankings have limitations. They favour institutions with strong research systems, international networks, reliable data and the capacity to participate effectively in global evaluation mechanisms.
A university's social contribution, teaching culture, affordability, accessibility and influence on national intellectual life cannot always be reduced to a numerical position or ranking band. Nor should a university become obsessed with improving its ranking at the expense of educating students.
Yet dismissing rankings altogether would be equally unwise. International rankings may be imperfect, but they provide benchmarks that universities can use to identify institutional weaknesses.
They force universities to ask difficult questions about research productivity, citation impact, doctoral programmes, international collaboration, industry connections and academic governance. These are not meaningless concerns.
Perhaps the most important lesson from the latest ranking is therefore not that private universities are defeating public universities. It is that the old public-private divide is becoming less useful for understanding academic performance.
A university should be judged increasingly by what it produces, how it teaches, how it researches, how it engages with society and how effectively it prepares students for a changing world.
There is another issue that deserves attention. Some universities participated in the ranking but did not receive a final numerical position because they had not met the necessary conditions.
They were instead placed in the "reporter" category. This is significant because participation itself indicates that institutions are becoming conscious of the importance of international benchmarking. But participation should be the beginning, not the achievement.
The real challenge is to build the academic systems required to move from reporting data to demonstrating sustained performance.
For private universities, the latest results should bring confidence, but also caution. Ranking success can easily become a marketing slogan. A university that enters an international ranking today can fall out tomorrow if its research culture stagnates.
Sustainable academic reputation cannot be built through advertising campaigns, impressive buildings or expensive programs alone. It requires serious faculty recruitment, academic freedom, research funding, ethical governance, strong libraries and laboratories, rigorous assessment, and an environment in which teachers are encouraged to produce knowledge rather than merely deliver courses.
Public universities face a different but equally important challenge. Their historical advantages remain substantial, but history cannot function as an automatic ranking mechanism.
Public universities possess enormous intellectual resources and some of the country's finest scholars. What they need is an institutional environment capable of converting those resources into stronger research, better international collaboration, and more consistent academic output.
The real winner, if the trend continues, could be Bangladeshi higher education itself. Competition can force institutions to improve. A student should not have to choose between the prestige of an old university and the modernity of a new one. Ideally, every university should be compelled to offer both intellectual depth and contemporary academic opportunities.
The rise of private universities should therefore not be viewed as the decline of public universities. It should be viewed as a warning against the idea that reputation is inherited permanently.
Universities, like ideas, must continually prove their relevance. Bangladesh's higher education system will advance when institutions stop asking who traditionally occupied the top and start asking who is doing the work required to deserve it.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.
